title: Southeast Airlines 308
summary: A Douglas DC-3A operated by Southeast Airlines crashed into the Holston Mountain range during approach to Tri-Cities Regional Airport in Bristol, Tennessee on January 8, 1959, killing all 10 occupants. The flight encountered visibility of 3 miles in light snow and fog with a 900-foot broken ceiling. The crew reported problems with the automatic direction finder and were unable to locate the outer marker. The aircraft descended below safe altitude and struck the wooded slope.

title: American Airlines 320
summary: American Airlines Flight 320, a Lockheed L-188 Electra flying from Chicago to New York, crashed into the East River about 4,900 ft short of runway 22 while approaching LaGuardia Airport through a 400 ft overcast ceiling and fog, killing 65 of 73 aboard. The Civil Aeronautics Board found the crew, new to the Electra, flew below the intended approach path while the altimeter appeared to show a safe altitude; the Air Line Pilots Association instead blamed faulty instruments. It was the first crash involving the Electra type.
probable_cause: The Civil Aeronautics Board concluded the crew made mistakes that caused the crash, with the crew's inexperience on the Electra and poor weather conditions cited as contributing factors.

title: The Day the Music Died
summary: A Beechcraft Bonanza piloted by Roger Peterson departed Mason City at 00:55 on February 3, 1959 in poor wintry weather with ceiling 3000 ft, visibility 6 miles, and wind 20 mph gusting over 30 mph. Shortly after takeoff in conditions of fog and snow, the pilot lost accurate perception of aircraft attitude or motion and did not maintain control. The aircraft impacted terrain in a nose-down attitude near Clear Lake, Iowa, killing all four occupants including musicians Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens and J.P. Richardson.

title: 1959 Air Charter Turkey crash
summary: On 23 April 1959, a Avro Super Trader IV cargo aircraft registered G-AGRH departed Ankara en route to Bahrain as part of a long cargo flight from the United Kingdom to Woomera in Australia. The unpressurized aircraft was carrying twelve men and equipment for the Woomera rocket range. While flying on instruments over mountainous terrain between Ankara and Teheran, the aircraft drifted north of its assigned track due to strong winds. Sub-normal temperatures also resulted in high indicated altimeter readings, further contributing to the crew's altitude confusion. The aircraft crashed into Mount Süphan six days later during a search. The investigation concluded that strong winds and inaccurate wind forecasts, combined with altimeter errors from temperature effects and navigation problems, caused the accident.

title: TWA 891
summary: A Lockheed L-1649A Starliner carrying 59 passengers and 9 crew departed Milan Malpensa for Paris on June 26, 1959 in light rain and thunderstorms. Twelve minutes after takeoff while climbing through 10,000 feet, the aircraft suffered structural failure and broke up in mid-air. An Italian inquiry determined that a lightning strike ignited flammable vapors in fuel tank number 7, causing explosions that destroyed the aircraft structure.

title: American Airlines 514
summary: A Boeing 707-123 training flight from New York crashed near Calverton airfield during approach practice. The aircraft made a left bank to 45 degrees, then a progressive right bank until inverted with nose dropping. All five crew members aboard were killed in the crash. The probable cause was the crew's failure to recognize and correct excessive yaw that caused an unintentional rolling maneuver at too low an altitude for recovery.

title: National Airlines 967
summary: National Airlines Flight 967, a Douglas DC-7B, disappeared over the Gulf of Mexico en route from Tampa to New Orleans. At 12:44 AM, the captain reported a smooth flight with unlimited visibility but noted a solid overcast of fog ahead. The aircraft was cleared to descend to 5,000 feet, but the control tower reported actual ceiling of 1,200 feet with visibility of three-fourths mile in light fog and rain. Radar picked up the flight at 12:46 AM and observed it turn toward New Orleans, then the aircraft disappeared from radar at 12:51 AM and never responded to subsequent radio calls. All 42 aboard were presumed killed.

title: Aeroflot 315 (1959)
summary: Aeroflot Flight 315 crashed short of Lviv Airport runway during final approach in icing conditions. The aircraft descended normally in cold weather with humidity 97%, switched to visual flight rules after descending through clouds, and at 110 meters altitude the flaps were set to 45 degrees. The aircraft then experienced a rapid pitch down and crashed 2100 meters from the runway in a 25-degree nose-down attitude.
probable_cause: Anomaly in the engine power control system combined with substandard placement of cockpit controls; pitot tube icing caused erroneous airspeed readings; icing of the horizontal stabilizer created a supercritical angle of attack when flaps lowered to 45 degrees.

title: TWA 595

location.name: residential area southeast of Chicago-Midway Airport

summary: TWA Flight 595, a Lockheed Super Constellation cargo flight, received a fire warning in No. 2 engine shortly after departure from Chicago-Midway. The crew attempted to return for landing but at 600 feet on approach, the aircraft banked in excess of 45 degrees and began rapidly sinking. During their recovery attempt, the crew retracted the landing flaps, which resulted in a critical loss of lift. The aircraft impacted a residential area at 5:35 am CST, killing all 3 crewmembers and 8 people on the ground. Investigation revealed no actual fire in engine No. 2.
probable_cause: The aircraft received a false fire warning in engine No. 2. While attempting to return to Chicago-Midway from low altitude, the crew banked excessively exceeding 45 degrees during the turn to final approach at 600 feet. The aircraft began rapidly sinking, and the crew retracted the landing flaps during recovery, which resulted in loss of lift and prevented recovery from the descent. Several hundred feet would have been necessary to acquire enough airspeed to recover from the sinking condition.
